guarantees.claim: When state_sel == STATE_INIT, state_d is driven with state_init_i.
When state_sel == STATE_ROUND, state_d is driven with add_round_key_out.
When state_sel == STATE_CLEAR, state_d is driven with prd_clearing_state_i.
When state_sel is not one of the enumerated states and key_len_i == AES_256, state_d is driven with prd_clearing_state_i.
guarantees.cond: state_sel != STATE_INIT && state_sel != STATE_ROUND && state_sel != STATE_CLEAR && key_len_i == AES_256

guarantees.claim: When state_sel is not one of the enumerated states and key_len_i != AES_256, state_d is self-driven (state_d = state_d), creating a combinational hold.

formal_sketch.consequent: state_d is self-driven (state_d = state_d), creating a combinational hold

assumptions.claim: If state_sel takes a value outside {STATE_INIT, STATE_ROUND, STATE_CLEAR}, then key_len_i must equal AES_256.
assumptions.risk: If violated, state_d self-holds (combinational loop) and may retain secret intermediate AES state, bypassing the intended clearing.

uncertain_points.claim: Can state_sel ever be a value outside {STATE_INIT, STATE_ROUND, STATE_CLEAR} while key_len_i != AES_256? The default self-hold could leave secret state uncleared.
uncertain_points.risk: Secret AES state survives clearing attempts; potential leakage across encryptions or through debug/observation channels.

uncertain_points.claim: prd_clearing_state_i is used for clearing in STATE_CLEAR and in the default path when AES_256 is selected. Is its randomness/entropy sufficient to prevent secret state reconstruction?
uncertain_points.risk: If prd_clearing_state_i is predictable or constant, the clearing may be ineffective, leaving sensitive key/state information vulnerable to extraction.

formal_sketch.consequent: prd_clearing_state_i is used for clearing in STATE_CLEAR and in the default path when AES_256 is selected. Is its randomness/entropy sufficient to prevent secret state reconstruction?

security_implications: This state multiplexer directly drives the AES cipher state (state_d) which holds round key and intermediate encryption data. A default fallback when state_sel is outside the three enumerated states and key_len_i != AES_256 causes state_d to self-hold, potentially retaining secret material and defeating any clearing attempt. In the AES_256 case the same illegal state_sel drives a (pseudo-random) clearing value, but the clearing quality depends on prd_clearing_state_i. An unexpected state_sel could therefore expose uncleared secrets or mis-clear sensitive data, impacting confidentiality and correctness.
